doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: Sitting in at the Mocambo and Oscar Pettiford hearing him
summary: At a Monday morning session at the Chess brothers' Mocambo, Ware plays and Pettiford, who was in the house, asks his name.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: People don't know about Chris Anderson Henderson.

Not really. You know, I was a shy dude; I was afraid of the big name stars, and they come through, I was just afraid to be around them. I remember I went to a session one morning down at a place called the Mocambo -- it was a real swinging street; 39th and Cottage Grove in Chicago. And they had clubs back to back and everybody was having Monday morning jam sessions then. And that would go on all morning and all day, up until late at night.

However, this particular morning, I would come in the club, the Mocambo, a little bar, it was owned by Leonard and Phil Chess, who later had the Chess recording company -- and I used to work Monday nights there.

But anyway, I go in there and it's morning -- with and Malachi and a couple of the guys we were hanging out with, and the bandstand was kind of full -- and Flip the trumpet player, we went to school together -- he was working with Red Saunders' band at the time -- he's up jamming, and he says, "C'mon, come up on stage; come up and play" -- you know. So the bass player gave up the fiddle and I end up playing, and we had a good groove going on, and I noticed they pushed me out in front, you know? Go solo. I'm Not much of a solo, but I do what I want to do. And I don't realize that Oscar Pettiford is in the house. He's sitting across -- I'm behind the bar playing, you know, with the cats -- and they tell me that when

I started playing, Pettiford had been sitting up there with his head down on the table, you know, between some other musicians, and when I started playing, he raised his head up and started listening.

So when I finished playing, I was getting ready to come down, the trumpet player, Flip, said, "Did you know that Oscar Pettiford is in the house?" -- and I felt like going through the floor; I had that much respect for the man, you know. And I'm trying to get out from under the bar, behind the bar, you know, coming out and Pettiford was coming in to meet me. He says, "Hey, wait a minute; hold it -- what's your name?"

I told him my name, and I'm stuttering -- not knowing what to say. He says, "I want you to come back to the hotel tomorrow." He was in town with Louis Bellson up on the North Side, and I said, "Okay" -- but I wasn't about to go. As a matter of fact, I said we're going in the morning. I said, oh man, you know.

Anyway, the next morning, he was at my house at 9 o'clock, and he said, "Man, we're going to see Pettiford" -- and I said, "Oh, man, I got to go somewhere else and do this." And he said, "No, we're going up there." And I did go -- went by there. He got up and he showed me, he says, "Wilbur, I like your bass playing, man." I mean, it was real beautiful just to talk to him, and he showed me -- he got out a cello and he says "I'm gonna amplify this and I'm gonna play it." So when

I first met him -- you know, that cat was beautiful. There he is when I come to New York, I didn't have a fiddle but he gave me one of his fiddles -- that's before he went to Europe. Oh, that's a long story. But that was one of the people that I met, you know.

Like I say, I was kind of shy in meeting the big names. Those fellows would come in and they'd walk in the club, and they'd kind of look down their noses at you. They don't know you -- you don't have no big name; they looked down their noses at you, you know. And actually, most of the Chicago musicians seemed like they were just waiting. They'd say, "Okay, you kind of snubbing me, huh?" But then they'd get up there and play, and then they would win the respect of the man, you know.
